title: Quantum Financial Modeling on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum Hardware: Random Walks using Approximate Quantum Counting
abstract_summary: The paper introduces approximate quantum counting circuits that use far fewer two-qubit entangling gates than traditional binary-encoded quantum counting, enabling more noise-robust tracking of position in quantum walks for financial modeling. The authors demonstrate these circuits' resilience on NISQ hardware, compare resulting price-change distributions to stock index data, and study the effect of mid-measurement (quantum Zeno-like behavior) with applications to housing market liquidity and volatility.
methodology_description: The study designs and evaluates approximate quantum counting circuits as alternatives to binary positional counters for tracking position in quantum walks. Several circuit families are proposed and implemented: arc counter (rotation encoding using only single-qubit rotations), arc walk (Hadamard coin controlling rotations), random-jump counters (selecting a target counter qubit per step with a weighted distribution), and cascading-disjunction components (Toffoli-based Boolean OR propagation). Circuits were evaluated in three environments: ideal (noise-free) simulation, noisy simulation (simulator with expected gate noise models), and on an 11-qubit trapped-ion QPU (Wright et al. 2019). Experiments measured output distributions and average distances after varying numbers of steps, compared results across circuit types (including a traditional binary counter baseline), and examined effects of mid-circuit measurement (Quantum Zeno effect) by inserting measurements at different frequencies. Financial comparisons included distributional comparisons of simulated relative price-change outputs to 5 years of Dow Jones daily returns (Yahoo! Finance) and an empirical analysis of Zillow housing summary statistics (monthly metro-area sales counts, list-to-sale price ratios, ZHVI). Random-jump circuits introduced classical randomness in circuit construction (multiple random circuit instances) and outputs were aggregated (averaging across shots and across sampled circuits). Statistical analyses included fitted normal distributions for comparisons and Pearson correlations (sales count vs list-to-sale ratio) for the Zillow data.

circuit_design: Define counter register and coin qubit(s).
Arc counter: apply single-qubit rotations on counter qubits with angles halving by significance (rotation encoding).
Arc walk: apply Hadamard to coin; conditionally apply controlled rotations on counter qubits when coin=|1>.

Random-jump: for each step, sample a target qubit according to weighted distribution (prefer low-order qubits), flip or rotate that qubit conditioned on coin; repeat for multiple randomly-generated circuits.
Cascading disjunction: insert Toffoli-based OR gates between selected lower- and higher-order bits to propagate ones upward; requires ancilla and mid-circuit reset for reuse.

reproducibility_notes: The paper describes circuit designs, parameter choices (qubit counts, shot counts, step counts) and the data sources used (Yahoo! Finance for Dow Jones; Zillow Research for housing statistics). However, no code repository, circuit source code, or exact noisy simulator configuration is provided in the preprint. Mid-circuit-reset and measurement availability is noted as platform-dependent. Reproducing results will require re-implementing the described circuits (arc counter, arc walk, random-jump, cascading disjunction), choosing or matching the simulator noise model, and using the specified shot/circuit sampling regimes. Datasets referenced are publicly available, but exact date ranges and any small preprocessing choices (e.g., exact months included per metro) are not fully enumerated in the paper.
key_findings: [supported] Approximate quantum counting circuits (rotation/arc encodings and variants) can be implemented with far fewer 2-qubit entangling gates than traditional binary-positional quantum counting (Toffoli-based) circuits.

[supported] The approximate counting circuits (arc counter, arc walk, random-jump, cascading-disjunction) are more robust to realistic/noisy hardware and noisy simulation than a straightforward binary counter: binary-counting circuits rapidly degrade on NISQ hardware while arc/count-based designs remain closer to ideal.

[supported] Empirical simulations and runs on an 11-qubit trapped-ion QPU show that binary counters become effectively useless after a few increments, whereas arc-counter circuits keep producing monotonic-like increases close to the ideal simulation.

[supported] The approximate counting circuits produce distributions of price changes (under the presented parametrizations and averaging) that display heavier tails similar to observed stock-index daily-change distributions (example: Dow Jones comparison shown).

[supported] Mid-circuit measurement (partial/decohering measurements) reduces the expected distance traveled by the quantum-walk-like circuits (demonstrated in simulation), consistent with a quantum Zeno–type effect; example: 20-step walk mean positions were 35.6 (no mid-measure), 14.3 (measurement every 7 steps), and 5.7 (measurement every step).

[supported] Analysis of Zillow housing-summary data finds that, in metro-months where average sale price < average list price, lower transaction counts are strongly correlated with larger list-to-sale price disparities (interpreted as lower liquidity associated with higher pricing uncertainty).
[supported] Cascading-disjunction components (a light-weight propagation technique) added to approximate counters increase and preserve progress in the walk (demonstrated in simulations).

[speculative] Approximate counting circuits sacrifice exact arithmetic and positional correctness but are argued to be acceptable for many economic modeling tasks (such as belief distributions and option-pricing inputs) because approximate, monotonic, scale-preserving behavior is often sufficient.

[speculative] Such approximate, lower-entanglement circuits could enable useful quantum-finance modeling on NISQ-era hardware before the advent of full fault-tolerant quantum computers (i.e., an early practical use-case pathway).

[speculative] The behavior of quantum walks with variable measurement frequency may capture economically-relevant phenomena (e.g., markets with low transaction rates exhibiting higher volatility), suggesting a potential modeling role for quantum walks in macro/market dynamics.

[supported] Practical NISQ constraints (limited qubits, gate fidelity, especially 2-qubit entangling gate errors) severely limit traditional binary quantum counting approaches; this motivates designs that avoid heavy use of entangling gates.
results_summary: The paper introduces and evaluates several approximate quantum counting circuits (arc/rotation-encoded counters, arc-walks, random-jump counters, and cascading-disjunction variants) intended to track position in quantum-walk-style simulations while using far fewer 2-qubit entangling gates than binary-positional adders. Through ideal simulation, noisy simulation, and runs on an 11-qubit trapped-ion QPU, the authors show that traditional binary counters quickly fail under realistic noise, whereas their approximate designs remain close to ideal for many steps. They also demonstrate that mid-circuit (frequent) measurements reduce walk dispersion (quantum-Zeno-like behavior) and show an empirical housing-market correlation consistent with the hypothesis that lower transaction volumes associate with greater price uncertainty.
performance_claims: In ideal simulations (6-qubit counter register), average distances after n steps follow exact integers for binary counter and more gradual increases for arc/random schemes (detailed in Table 1).

In noisy simulation and on an 11-qubit trapped-ion QPU, binary counter outputs quickly converge to a near-random average around ~32 (for a 6-qubit register representing 0–63), while arc-counter QPU outputs remain close to ideal incremental behavior (see Table 2 and Figure 16).
Arc-counter and arc-walk circuits used 1000 shots per job in experiments; random-jump experiments used 30 circuits × 30 shots (introducing classical-programming randomness).
Example mid-measurement effect: for a 20-step arc-counter walk, mean positions observed in simulation were 35.6 (no measurement), 14.3 (measurement every 7 steps), and 5.7 (measurement every step).

Zillow housing-data analysis: for metro-months where avg sale price < avg list price, Pearson correlations between monthly sales counts and list-to-sale ratios are 'nearly all strongly positive' (histogram shown in Figure 19) indicating lower counts correlate with larger list-to-sale disparities.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper demonstrates that approximate counting circuits are more NISQ-robust than binary-positional counters (empirical, small-scale evidence), but it does not demonstrate a provable or general quantum computational advantage. The suggestion that these circuits could enable useful quantum-finance applications on NISQ hardware prior to fault-tolerance is a plausible but speculative claim requiring further quantitative validation at larger scales.
limitations: NISQ-era hardware constraints: limited qubit counts and gate accuracies (especially 2-qubit entangling gates) make deep/entangling circuits unreliable.
Traditional binary positional quantum counting (adder/Toffoli-based) requires many entangling gates and quickly becomes unusable on current hardware.
Approximate counting circuits are inherently statistical and produce noisy outputs from a mix of quantum randomness, classical randomness in circuit construction, and hardware noise.
Some proposed approximate circuits (e.g. arc counter) do not support exact decrementing or exact integer semantics — they are approximate representations of position.
Approximate circuits (e.g. arc counter) do not provide a quantum computational advantage in some cases because they are easy to simulate classically.
Prototype designs lack the mathematical guarantees and elegant operator correspondences (no unit increment/decrement ladder operators as in exact quantum walkers).

Mid-circuit measurement and mid-circuit reset support varies across platforms; certain constructions (e.g. cascading disjunction requiring mid-circuit reset) are not guaranteed to be implementable everywhere.
Classical simulation of ideal quantum circuits is tractable only for small numbers of qubits, limiting the ability to validate and extrapolate behaviour to larger circuits on classical hardware.
Empirical experiments reported used a small older trapped-ion QPU (11 qubits); results may not generalize to larger/more recent hardware without further testing.
Some approximate designs produce representational artifacts (e.g. peaks at certain values, such as powers of two) that may require smoothing or further mitigation.
[inferred] Scalability to large numbers of steps/large position registers is uncertain — robustness observed for small registers/steps may not hold at larger scales.
[inferred] Classical randomness introduced in circuit generation (e.g. random jump selection) may bias distributions in non-transparent ways and needs careful analysis.
[inferred] No comprehensive benchmark comparing approximate-counting approaches against state-of-the-art optimized binary adders (e.g. Cuccaro, Gidney) on modern hardware is presented.
[inferred] Hardware/topology-dependent effects (e.g. superconducting vs trapped-ion differences in gate fidelities/connectivity) and their impact on the proposed circuits are not explored.
